items.title: [esa.int] Hubble and Webb expose hidden structures in Carina star-forming cloud
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes have captured complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a star-forming pillar in the Carina Nebula about 7,500 light-years from Earth. Hubble’s visible-light image shows a dark dust column edged by glowing gas, while Webb’s infrared observations reveal details within the dust, including stars and fine strands. The images, released Oct. 29, help astronomers examine how young stars form in gas and dust exposed to radiation from massive nearby stars. Ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds likely shaped the pillar’s outline by eroding its surroundings, while denser material resisted erosion. Webb also imaged the lower-metallicity N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while Chandra and Webb observations show young stars forming in a separate Carina cloud.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] COP17 urges subsidy cuts as nature finance gap persists before COP31
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

items.title: [Fast Company] Colon cancer rates in the U.S. are on the rise for the first time in 20 years. Here’s who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

If you’re overdue for a colonoscopy, let this be your reminder: Colorectal cancer rates are increasing for pretty much everyone.

While word has gotten out about rising colorectal cancer rates among younger adults, a new study found that rates are climbing across all age groups up to the age of 69. Researchers from the University of Chicago found that the overall incidence rate for this type of cancer—the second-leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S.—rose for the first time in more than 20 years, according to a study published earlier this week in NEJM Evidence.

The age-adjusted incidence rate of colorectal cancer rose from 36.7 per 100,000 people in 2022 to 38.3 in 2023, the study authors found. By comparison, the incidence rate in 2000 was 55.2. The incidence rate among people between the ages of 45 and 49 rose nearly 13% from 2019 to 2023, the sharpest increase among any age group—although that’s likely driven by more people in this cohort undergoing screenings. In 2021, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force lowered the recommended age for a first screening from 50 to 45.

“That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do—it’s catching cancer earlier,” Caitlin Murphy, the lead author of the study and a professor of pediatrics and public health sciences at the University of Chicago, said in a statement. 

But earlier screening doesn’t explain why the incidence rate is also rising among older adults between the ages of 65 and 69, as they’re about 80% up to date with screenings and historically benefitted from this detection method. The results suggest that unknown risk factors may be offsetting the previous gains from screening—and the study’s authors say they still need to understand why that’s happening.

“In terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now causing it to increase in older people as well,” Murphy said.

THEORIES FOR THE ROOT CAUSE

Finding that root cause of colorectal cancer remains the biggest mystery for researchers to unravel. Earlier this year, new evidence showed that colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men and women under the age of 50. Meanwhile, nearly 160,000 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer this year, including both colon cancer and rectal cancer, according to estimates from the American Cancer Institute.

Theories for what causes colorectal cancer are wide ranging. A recent study found that faster biological aging could be a factor that’s associated with an increased risk of several early-onset cancers, including colorectal cancer. The authors of this latest study plan to explore another possible culprit: environmental chemical exposures.

Working with a toxicologist from Emory University, the team from the University of Chicago will measure thousands of environmental exposures to see which ones warrant further research, then test those chemicals on organoids, which are specialized models that can grow colons in a dish.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Neptune may have formed from building blocks that originated closer to the young Sun before moving outward, according to research published in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Neptune’s deep atmosphere appears considerably richer in oxygen than Uranus’s, despite the planets’ similar size and mass, suggesting different chemical histories. Researchers used carbon monoxide measurements and atmospheric models to infer the planets’ hidden chemistry; they cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres. The proposed formation pathway therefore depends on models. Future spacecraft observations or atmospheric probes could help test it. NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe is expected to launch sometime in the next decade.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

Proposals include improving water retention, adapting crops and linking farm credit to technical support. items.title: [tmtpost.com] AI reshapes work as layoffs, hiring gains and entry-level risks diverge
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Data-center construction is creating union jobs in Nevada, while automation cuts or threatens positions in hospitality and customer service and employers in other sectors increase output without expanding headcount. A report by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found little evidence of widespread AI-related job losses in the state so far, while a survey of Swiss finance chiefs found 64% expect fewer entry-level finance jobs over the next three years. In Nevada, self-driving vehicles, casino robots and digital guest services are changing work on the Las Vegas Strip as thousands of tradespeople build data centers near Reno. Analysts and researchers warn that companies may reduce junior hiring because AI handles basic tasks that traditionally helped new workers gain experience. A survey cited by MIT Technology Review Insights found 16% of respondents saw transformative value from AI, while 12% had agents in production. U.S. federal AI regulation remains stalled in Congress, but a local report said the next Congress could take it up in January. China’s State Council issued guidance on Oct. 23 to limit employment displacement and support worker transitions.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Oil majors report wartime profit surge as climate groups demand windfall taxes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Six major European oil companies earned a combined $89 billion in the first nine months of 2026, more than twice their earnings a year earlier. U.S. oil and gas companies made more than $130 billion from April through September, nearly three times their earnings in the same period last year. The companies benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins after the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran disrupted energy supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Climate campaigners called for windfall taxes, arguing the revenue should cushion households against energy costs and extreme weather and support a shift to cleaner energy. The oil and gas industry opposes a European Union-wide levy, warning it could weaken investment and energy security. The EU is considering such a tax, while Portugal has already imposed a 33% levy on extraordinary 2026 profits. Companies have largely used windfalls to reduce debt and return money to shareholders rather than increase production spending.
